questions.question: What does a 'right roll' of a die do to its faces?
options: Rotates the die 90 degrees to the right, moving the top face to the right side, the right face to the bottom, and so on in a cycle
Nothing, faces stay fixed
Swaps only the top and bottom faces
Rotates the die around a vertical axis only
questions.rationale: A right roll rotates the die 90 degrees to the right around its front-back axis, cycling top -> right -> bottom -> left -> top.

questions.question: What does a 'left roll' do, compared to a right roll?
options: Exactly the same thing as a right roll
Only rotates the die vertically
Rotates the die 90 degrees in the opposite direction, cycling the faces the reverse way around the same axis
Has no effect on the die's faces
questions.rationale: A left roll cycles the same set of faces (top, right, bottom, left) but in the reverse direction compared to a right roll.

questions.question: What does a 'backward roll' (or forward roll) rotate the die around, compared to left/right rolls?
options: The exact same axis as left/right rolls
A different axis — front-to-back rather than left-to-right — cycling the top, front, and bottom faces instead
No axis at all
Only the die's color, not its faces
questions.rationale: Forward/backward rolls rotate around the left-right axis, cycling the top, front, bottom, and back faces — a different set from the left/right roll's top-right-bottom-left cycle.

questions.question: What is a 'rotation cycle memory chart' used for?
options: Tracking the die's color changes
Only used for symbol dice, not numbered ones
Listing the die's manufacturing date
Summarizing which face moves to which position for each type of roll (right, left, forward, backward), as a quick reference
questions.rationale: This chart consolidates exactly how each roll type (right, left, forward, backward) cycles the faces, providing a quick reference instead of re-deriving it each time.

questions.question: After a 180-degree rotation around a given axis, what happens to the face that was on top?
options: It moves to the position directly opposite where it started (e.g., top becomes bottom)
It stays on top
It becomes hidden permanently
It swaps with a random side face
questions.rationale: A full 180-degree rotation around an axis moves a face to the position diametrically opposite its starting point — top becomes bottom, for instance.

questions.question: What is a 'rotation invariant' in dice reasoning?
options: A face that changes with every rotation
A die that cannot be rotated
A property (like which faces are opposite each other) that stays the same no matter how the die is rotated
A rule that only applies to symbol dice
questions.rationale: A rotation invariant is a property, like the set of opposite-face pairs, that remains fixed regardless of how the die is physically rotated.

questions.question: What does an 'impossible position test' check for?
options: Whether the die has the correct number of faces
Whether a proposed arrangement of faces could ever actually occur through valid rotations of the real die, ruling out impossible answer options
The physical weight of the die
Whether the die's color is valid
questions.rationale: This test checks whether a proposed face arrangement could actually be reached through valid rotations of the real die, which is a powerful way to eliminate impossible answer options.

questions.question: What does a 'two-face adjacency test' verify?
options: Whether two faces are the same color
Whether the die is a standard numbered die
The total number of faces on the die
Whether two specific faces can validly be adjacent to each other, based on what's already known about the die's layout
questions.rationale: This test verifies whether two specific faces can validly be adjacent, checked against the adjacency and opposite relationships already established for the die.

questions.question: What does a 'three-face compatibility test' check, beyond a two-face adjacency test?
options: Nothing additional — they check the same thing
Whether three specific faces could all validly meet together at the same corner, not just whether each pair is individually adjacent
Only the color of the three faces
Whether the three faces are all even numbers
questions.rationale: This test goes further than pairwise adjacency, checking whether all three faces together could genuinely meet at one shared corner of the cube.

questions.question: What is the purpose of using a 'reference corner' for orientation?
options: To make the problem more confusing
To have one fixed, known point of reference from which all other face positions and rotations can be consistently tracked
To eliminate the need for any rotation rules
To only apply to symbol dice
questions.rationale: A fixed reference corner provides a consistent anchor point, letting all subsequent rotations and face positions be tracked relative to it rather than drifting inconsistently.
